Estimators: weights p(y)/q(y) with inclusion probability q = 1 - exp(-exp(phi - kappa)), kappa = (k+1)-th largest perturbed score; self-normalised version biased but consistent and lower variance. - input / output: autoregressive model with normalised conditional probabilities; k sampled sequences.
training: none (inference sampler / estimator); no gradient estimator in this paper.
results: k = 5, 10, 20 and T 0.1 - 0.8: better mean and maximum BLEU at equal diversity than diverse beam search; estimation variance below Monte Carlo for T < 0.5.
compute: linear in k and sequence length.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - stochastic exploration of the beam in training (different nodes survive in different epochs).
compat_needs: normalised conditional probabilities child | parent.
compat_conflicts: our validity scores are independent survival products, not normalised conditionals.

name: Unordered-set estimator (unbiased gradients from k samples without replacement)
papers: Estimating Gradients for Discrete Random Variables by Sampling without Replacement (Kool, van Hoof, Welling, ICLR 2020) https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.06043 (read via ar5iv; last 29 k characters not read)
idea: An unbiased estimator of expectations (and policy gradients) over discrete variables from a set of k samples drawn without replacement (Gumbel-top-k / stochastic beam search); a Rao-Blackwellisation of single-sample and importance-weighted estimators.
formulation: sum over the sampled set of p(s) * R(S^k, s) * f(s), R = leave-one-out ratio (probability of the other samples under the distribution restricted to D minus {s}, divided by the probability of the full set); a second-order leave-one-out ratio gives a built-in baseline with no extra evaluation; for sequences use stochastic beam search; exact set probability in O(2^k) or by numerical integration (naive O(k!)). - input / output: a discrete policy -> unbiased gradient.
training: REINFORCE-type; combined with pathwise terms if f depends on theta.
differentiable: yes in expectation (unbiased score-function gradient), not through the discrete choice.
sensors_data: Bernoulli toy, categorical VAE (10^2 and 10^20 latent states), TSP with 20 nodes.
results: lowest or comparable gradient variance in all three; categorical VAE on par with REINFORCE with replacement; TSP better than REINFORCE with replacement, stochastic sum-and-sample and a greedy rollout baseline, on par with a biased risk estimator.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - the only unbiased route found for training a stochastic top-b / top-M selection, at the price of normalised sampling probabilities.
compat_needs: normalised probabilities of the candidates; an episode-level reward.
compat_conflicts: policy-gradient variance; not needed if local supervision of scores exists.

name: Continuous relaxation of beam search (soft top-k beam trained end to end)
papers: A Continuous Relaxation of Beam Search for End-to-end Training of Neural Sequence Models (Goyal, Dyer, Berg-Kirkpatrick, AAAI 2018) https://arxiv.org/abs/1708.00111 (read via ar5iv)
idea: Replace the hard top-k of beam search by a soft top-k built from k peaked softmaxes; the beam state is a convex combination of previous states and expected input embeddings, so a task loss can be applied to the beam output. The temperature alpha is annealed up.
formulation: for rank i = 1..k: p_i = softmax over candidates of -alpha * (s - max_i)^2 with max_i the i-th largest score (iterated max operations); soft backpointer = row sums of p_i; new hidden state = backpointer-weighted average of previous hidden states; next input = expected embedding a_i^T E; cumulative score s_{t+1,i} = sum(s~_t * p_i). Loss: per-step Hamming loss accumulated along the soft beam, final loss = peaked softmax over final beam scores applied to the accumulated loss (soft max-margin variant worse). alpha annealed from non-peaked to peaked (constant 1.0 worse, large constant unstable in pilots); beam size 3, 50 epochs, warm start with cross-entropy. - input / output: sequence tagger (BiLSTM encoder, LSTM decoder, hidden 64 NER / 512 CCG); k label hypotheses.
training: regime `free_rollout` through the soft beam.
differentiable: yes at finite alpha (all candidates get gradient); hard beam recovered for alpha -> inf if no ties.
sensors_data: German NER (CoNLL 2003), CCG supertagging (CCGbank); no NMT experiment.
results: CCG tag accuracy: cross-entropy greedy 80.35, cross-entropy hard beam 82.42, soft-beam training 85.78 (soft) / 85.82 (hard beam at test); NER macro F1: 54.92 greedy cross-entropy vs 56.38 / 56.15.
compute: about k times cross-entropy training; flat objective with huge gradients near change points at high alpha.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - template for "prune M nodes per level with gradient"; state mixing is only defined for recurrent states, a convex combination of two positions is not a lane point.
compat_needs: scalar score per candidate; averageable states.
compat_conflicts: averaging node positions or tokens blends different lanes; cost grows with the number of soft selections.

name: Fully differentiable beam search decoder (beam as a computation graph, gold paths added to the normaliser)
papers: A Fully Differentiable Beam Search Decoder (Collobert, Hannun, Synnaeve, ICML 2019) https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.06022 (read via ar5iv)
idea: Express the decoder (lexicon, transition and word-LM scores, merging of equal hypotheses by logadd, pruning to a beam) as differentiable operations and train the acoustic model through it with a sequence-level criterion; the gold alignments are always included in the normaliser.
formulation: per hypothesis (lexicon state, LM state, score); equal states merged with logadd; beam keeps the top scores (discrete; no gradient through the top-K decision, gradient through the scores of the kept hypotheses); loss = -( logadd over gold alignments (Forward) - log( beam sum - beam-gold sum + gold-alignment sum ) ) (Eq. 8); too small a beam diverges; beam 500 mostly (1000, 2000 tested). - input / output: frame token scores -> word sequence.
training: beam-level criterion; regime `free_rollout` through the beam output.
differentiable: partial - pruning hard; gradient through kept scores only.
results: WSJ test WER: ASG 10 M model beam 8000 5.6; DBD 10 M beam 500 5.9; DBD 7.5 M beam 500 5.3, beam 1000 5.1; acoustic-only ASG 4-gram 11.3 vs DBD 4-gram 9.9.
compute: epoch 35 / 90 / 180 min at beam 500 / 1000 / 2000; CPU-only criterion; custom implementation about 10x faster than autograd.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort L - portable lesson: put the labelled hypothesis into the normaliser so that the gold path never leaves the beam during training (gold-in-beam).
compat_needs: additive path scores, logadd merging of equal states.
compat_conflicts: continuous positions need a clustering rule to define "equal states" (our DAG conversion).

name: Differentiable particle filters: gradient stop at resampling (Jonschkowski) and soft resampling (Karkus)
papers: Differentiable Particle Filters: End-to-End Learning with Algorithmic Priors (Jonschkowski, Rastogi, Brock, RSS 2018) https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11122; Particle Filter Networks with Application to Visual Localization (Karkus, Hsu, Lee, CoRL 2018) https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.08975 (both read via ar5iv)
idea: Resampling is the beam cut of a particle filter. Jonschkowski: resampling by stochastic universal sampling is not differentiable and simply stops the gradient after one loop iteration, so effects of earlier steps on the current belief are neglected. Karkus: soft resampling draws ancestors from a mixture of the weight distribution and a uniform one and corrects with importance weights, keeping a gradient path.
formulation: Jonschkowski loss = -log of the Gaussian-mixture density of the true state under the weighted particles; components pre-trained, then end to end on overlapping subsequences (length 20 global localisation, 50 KITTI); 100 particles train, 1000 test. Karkus: q(k) = alpha * w_k + (1 - alpha)/K, new weight w' = w / (alpha w + (1 - alpha)/K) (alpha value not extracted); K = 30 particles in training with no resampling there; squared-error loss on the weighted mean pose; BPTT limited to 4 steps (1 / 2 / 4 steps: 73 / 79 / 79 % success). - input / output: weighted particle set.
training: end to end through the filter.
differentiable: partial - ancestor choice has no gradient (Jonschkowski); soft resampling keeps the weight dependency but stays biased.
sensors_data: simulated mazes, KITTI visual odometry (Jonschkowski); House3D (Karkus).
results: KITTI translational error (m/m), test 100: BKF 0.2062, DPF independent 0.1901, end to end 0.1467 +- 0.0149; House3D tracking RMSE PF-net 40.5 cm vs histogram filter 92.0, LSTM 66.9, odometry 109.4. Resampling helped under high uncertainty (39 -> 42 %) but hurt tracking in training (79 -> 75 %). Neither paper discusses particle collapse or bias explicitly.
compute: about 0.6 ms per particle per step (RGB PF-net).
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort S - cheap but biased; at least shows that training with and without the cut differ by a few percent in a long-horizon task.
compat_needs: weights over a particle set.
compat_conflicts: bias; in the Karkus experiments resampling during training hurt tracking success (79 -> 75 %) while helping under high uncertainty (39 -> 42 %).

name: Differentiable particle filter via entropic optimal transport (resampling with gradient)
papers: Differentiable Particle Filtering via Entropy-Regularized Optimal Transport (Corenflos, Thornton, Deligiannidis, Doucet, ICML 2021) https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07850 (read via ar5iv; last 45 k characters not read)
idea: Replace the ancestor draw by the entropic optimal-transport map from the weighted particle set to the uniform one: each new particle is a weighted average of the old ones, so gradients reach all particles.
formulation: X~_i = N * sum_k P^OT_{eps,i,k} X_k (barycentric projection, Eq. 13); stabilised Sinkhorn (Feydy et al.), cost rescaled so eps is scale-free; eps = 0.5 default; O(N^2) per iteration; gradients by gradient stitching on the converged potentials or autodiff through the loop. Ignoring the resampling gradient gives a biased ELBO gradient (Prop. 4.1); the OT filter is consistent for eps_N = o(1/log N) under compactness assumptions (Prop. 4.3); the likelihood estimate is biased (only affine functions preserved). Soft resampling (alpha = 0.1) performed worse than plain PF and OT filter. - input / output: weighted particle set -> equally weighted set.
training: end to end (ELBO, proposal learning, VRNN, localisation).
sensors_data: linear Gaussian SSM, polyphonic music, maze localisation.
results: proposal learning (d = 25): parameter RMSE 0.11 for DPF (N = 25) vs 0.22 for PF (N = 500), ESS about 60 % vs 25 %; JSB test ELBO DPF -7.67, PF -7.92, soft PF -8.17; maze test MSE DPF 3.55 / 4.65 / 4.44 vs PF 10.71 / 11.86 / 12.88 and soft PF 9.14 / 10.12 / 11.42.
compute: O(N^2) per Sinkhorn iteration in training; plain O(N) filter afterwards.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - the beam cut with gradient to all nodes; barycentric merging averages positions, which blends different lanes unless the cost makes the transport local.
compat_needs: weights and a cost in a vector space.
compat_conflicts: averaged particles of different lanes are off-lane; bias; O(N^2).

name: Differentiable particle filtering without modifying the forward pass (stop-gradient reweighting)
papers: Differentiable Particle Filtering without Modifying the Forward Pass (Scibior, Wood, 2021) https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.10314 (read via ar5iv; last 28 k characters not read)
idea: Keep the hard resampling of the forward pass. Stop the gradient of the weights flowing into the resampling distribution and multiply each resampled particle's weight by v/stopgrad(v), which equals 1 in the forward pass; gradients then flow into the resulting weights.
formulation: automatic differentiation of the log-marginal-likelihood estimate recovers the score-function estimator of Poyiadjis et al.; unbiased for expectations under the unnormalised posterior (Theorem 1), consistent for the normalised one; the common practice of dropping resampling terms has a bias that does not vanish (citing Corenflos); marginal variant reduces variance from quadratic to linear in sequence length at quadratic cost in the particle number. - input / output: weighted particles.
training: linear Gaussian SSM (200 steps), VRNN on occluded 2-D images (40 steps).
differentiable: partial - forward hard, gradient to weights through the stop-gradient trick.
results: improves over standard PF with few particles and converges faster with many; on VRNN standard PF fits training data better but overfits, the new estimator is better on test; no numbers in the excerpt.
compute: small extra cost; the forward pass is unchanged.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort S - pattern for "hard top-M forward, multiplicative node weights carry the gradient of the downstream loss to the survivors' scores"; inconclusive for learning the proposal.
compat_needs: multiplicative weights on survivors.
compat_conflicts: dropped candidates still receive no gradient.

name: Straight-through estimators, Gumbel-softmax, ReinMax and the bias of the surrogate gradient
papers: Estimating or Propagating Gradients Through Stochastic Neurons for Conditional Computation (Bengio, Leonard, Courville, 2013) https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.3432 (not opened); Categorical Reparameterization with Gumbel-Softmax (Jang, Gu, Poole, ICLR 2017) https://arxiv.org/abs/1611.01144; Understanding Straight-Through Estimator in Training Activation Quantized Neural Nets (Yin et al., ICLR 2019) https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.05662; Bridging Discrete and Backpropagation: Straight-Through and Beyond (Liu et al., NeurIPS 2023, ReinMax) https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08612 (last three read via ar5iv)
idea: A hard decision in the forward pass with a surrogate derivative in the backward pass. Gumbel-softmax: y_i = exp((log pi_i + g_i)/tau) / sum_j exp((log pi_j + g_j)/tau); the ST variant uses the one-hot sample forward and the soft sample backward. Yin et al.: coarse gradients with a vanilla or clipped ReLU surrogate are positively correlated with the true population gradient (descent direction), the identity surrogate is not. ReinMax: ST is a first-order (forward Euler) approximation of the gradient w.r.t. the logits; the Heun-type correction is second-order.
formulation: ST gradient = (df/dD) * d softmax/d theta. ReinMax: grad = 2 * grad^((pi+D)/2) - 0.5 * grad^ST, via pi_0 = softmax(theta), D sample, pi_1 = (D + softmax_tau(theta))/2 with stop-gradient, pi_2 = 2 pi_1 - 0.5 pi_0 then the ST trick. Gumbel-softmax schedule tau = max(0.5, exp(-r t)) every N in {500, 1000} steps, r in {1e-5, 1e-4}; small tau gives near one-hot samples with high gradient variance, large tau smooth but biased. ST and ReinMax work better with tau >= 1; ST Gumbel-softmax with tau <= 1. - input / output: logits -> hard one-hot / k-hot.
training: end to end; ReinMax costs about the same time and memory as ST (5.2 s per epoch on MNIST-VAE).
differentiable: partial - the discrete choice has no gradient; the surrogate is biased (ST first-order, ST Gumbel-softmax biased).
sensors_data: SBN / VAE on MNIST, ListOps, polynomial programming, CIFAR ResNet-20 quantisation.
results: test NLL SBN (Cat.): ST 61.8, Gumbel-softmax 59.0, ST Gumbel-softmax 59.7; VAE (Cat.): ST 110.9, Gumbel-softmax 101.5, ST Gumbel-softmax 107.8. ResNet-20 4-bit activations: identity surrogate 54.16 %, vanilla ReLU 86.59 %, clipped ReLU 91.24 % (2-bit: 46.52 / 48.05 / 88.39). ListOps accuracy ReinMax 68.07 +- 1.18, STGS 67.30 +- 2.50, ST 66.26 +- 0.48; MNIST-VAE -ELBO ReinMax 103.21, ST 116.72. Yin et al.: a poor surrogate "generates coarse gradients incompatible with the energy landscape" (instability); proofs hold for the population loss (infinite samples) only.
compute: Gumbel-softmax / ST / ReinMax about equal cost.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort S - the generic fallback for any hard keep / pick decision in the tree; the choice of surrogate matters (identity can fail).
compat_needs: a differentiable surrogate of the decision.
compat_conflicts: bias; sensitivity to tau and surrogate shape.

name: Sparse top-k / top-1 routing with load balancing (Switch Transformer; noisy top-k gating)
papers: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity (Fedus, Zoph, Shazeer, JMLR 2022) https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.03961 (read via ar5iv; last 28 k characters not read); Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer (Shazeer et al., 2017) https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538 (not opened; described in the Switch paper)
idea: A router picks the highest-probability expert per token; the layer output is p_i(x) * E_i(x), so the gate value keeps the router differentiable although the choice is hard; an auxiliary loss keeps the load balanced and avoids collapse onto few experts.
formulation: p_i(x) = softmax(W_r x); output p_i(x) E_i(x) for the argmax expert; loss_aux = alpha * N * sum_i f_i * P_i, f_i = fraction of tokens dispatched to i, P_i = mean router probability, alpha = 1e-2; capacity = tokens/N * factor (1.0 - 1.25), overflow tokens pass by the residual (<1 % dropped). Shazeer: noisy top-k (k >= 2) with separate importance and load losses (from the Switch description). Instabilities: hard routing and bfloat16 in the router softmax; remedies: float32 router, initialisation scaled down 10x, expert dropout 0.4 in fine-tuning; Switch-XXL still sometimes unstable. - input / output: token features -> expert assignment.
training: end to end; regime `none`.
differentiable: partial - the choice is constant, gradient through the gate value of the chosen expert.
results: over 7x pre-training speed-up vs T5-Base at equal FLOPs per token; the page summary quotes steps 60 k and 450 k for a 64-expert Switch-Base against T5-Base, "about 7.5x" in steps (the direction of that sentence is ambiguous in the summary); dropped tokens typically < 1 %.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort S - the load-balancing term is a documented antidote to children / experts that never get used (slots collapsing), usable as "slot usage" regulariser over a batch of tips.
compat_needs: batch-level statistics f_i, P_i over the b slots.
compat_conflicts: forces uniform slot use, whereas forks are rare among tips - a uniform-usage prior is wrong for the second slot; use only as a weak term (the rate of forks per tip in our data was not looked up here).

name: Differentiable token pruning by a learned keep mask and attention masking (DynamicViT)
papers: DynamicViT: Efficient Vision Transformers with Dynamic Token Sparsification (Rao et al., NeurIPS 2021) https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.02034 (abstract and search summaries only; ar5iv conversion failed); extension: Dynamic Spatial Sparsification for Efficient Vision Transformers and Convolutional Neural Networks https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.01580 (search summary only)
idea: A lightweight prediction module scores token importance at several layers and prunes hierarchically; training stays end to end through an attention masking strategy that blocks interactions of pruned tokens differentiably (shapes stay fixed in training; tokens are removed physically at inference).
formulation: not read. From the search summaries: losses cross-entropy + distillation toward the unpruned backbone; extension: ratio loss weight 2, KL and distillation weights 0.5, keep ratios geometric [rho, rho^2, rho^3]. A Gumbel-softmax sampled binary mask (from memory, not confirmed on the pages seen). - input / output: token sequence -> pruned token sequence.
training: cross-entropy + distillation + ratio loss; regime `none`.
differentiable: partial (binary mask with a differentiable surrogate; from memory).
results: about 31 - 37 % FLOPs reduction and over 40 % throughput gain with an accuracy drop within 0.5 % (poster page summary).
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - the masking trick is the standard way to prune with fixed tensor shapes in training: dropped tree nodes stay in the tensor but are masked out of attention among siblings and from the loss.
compat_needs: attention among nodes (our cascade stage C).
compat_conflicts: needs a target keep ratio; details unread.

name: Beam-Search Optimization (BSO): margin loss on the beam, reset when the gold prefix falls off
papers: Sequence-to-Sequence Learning as Beam-Search Optimization (Wiseman, Rush, EMNLP 2016) https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.02960 (read via ar5iv)
idea: Train a sequence model with the beam search it is decoded with: whenever the gold prefix is not within the beam (margin violation), a margin loss pushes the gold prefix above the K-th beam entry; the beam is then reset to contain the gold prefix (LaSO-style) and search continues.
formulation: L(f) = sum_t Delta(y_hat_{1:t}^(K)) * [ 1 - f(y_t, h_{t-1}) + f(y_hat_t^(K), h_hat_{t-1}^(K)) ]; Delta = 0/1 (word ordering, parsing) or 1 - smoothed sentence BLEU (MT); f is an unnormalised score (removes label bias); pre-training with word-level cross-entropy needed (random init failed); beam curriculum from 2, +1 every 2 epochs up to K_tr; constrained beam search (ConBSO) with hard constraints in the successor function; gradients flow through the gold and violating prefixes (not through the whole beam); Adagrad, batch 64. - input / output: sequence model with scores; beam of prefixes.
training: regime `free_rollout` with reset (gold-in-beam).
differentiable: partial - top-K selection constant; gradient through the scores of gold and violating prefixes.
sensors_data: word ordering, dependency parsing, German-English MT.
results: word ordering BLEU (K_te = 10): seq2seq 31.0, BSO 34.3, ConBSO 34.5; dependency parsing UAS / LAS: 88.66 / 84.33 -> 91.17 / 87.41 (BSO), 91.57 / 87.26 (ConBSO); MT BLEU (K_te = 5): 24.03 -> 26.36.
compute: tokens/s 13,038 (seq2seq) vs 1,985 (K_tr = 2) and 1,458 (K_tr = 6); the stated 3.3x overhead is inconsistent with the K_tr = 2 figure (about 6.6x).
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - "reset" = insert the GT-nearest node into the beam when it was cut; margin loss needs an unnormalised score (our validity).
compat_needs: scores comparable across beam entries; a gold prefix (nearest-node sequence).
compat_conflicts: the gold prefix must exist as a node sequence in the tree.

name: Learning beam search policies via imitation learning (beam-aware losses, continue / reset / stop)
papers: Learning Beam Search Policies via Imitation Learning (Negrinho, Gormley, Gordon, NeurIPS 2018) https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.00512 (read via ar5iv; experiments section not reached)
idea: Treat the beam as part of the model: a scoring function ranks the neighbours of the beam elements, an oracle cost-to-go defines which neighbour is best, and surrogate losses on the beam are minimised on trajectories collected by the learned policy.
formulation: beam = up to k nodes; candidates A_b = all neighbours; keep top-k by score s(v, theta); cost-to-go c*(v); beam cost = min over elements; cost increase when the best completion falls out of the beam. Losses: perceptron (first) = early update; perceptron / margin (last); cost-sensitive margin (last) close to BSO; upper bound on expected transition cost; log losses normalised over the beam or over all neighbours. Data collection: oracle, stop (first cost increase), reset (to the oracle's best node, as LaSO), continue (keep following the learned policy, as DAgger, the new strategy), mixtures with weight beta. Theory: no-regret reduction (DAgger-style), bounds for stop and reset depend on how often the roll-in deviates. - input / output: any search space with scores and an oracle.
training: regime `dagger` (continue) / `free_rollout`; Adam or SGD; losses differentiable w.r.t. the scores (how gradients pass the beam selection is not detailed).
differentiable: partial - selection constant, loss on scores.
sensors_data: NLP tasks (not reached in the text read).
results: none seen.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - the clearest statement of training with the beam in the loop; continue (own beam) is our free roll-out, reset is gold-in-beam; the oracle cost-to-go can be a point-to-polyline residual of the subtree.
compat_needs: an oracle cost per node (distance to the GT lane graph).
compat_conflicts: needs the node scores to be comparable; loss choices matter (not tested for geometry).

name: Scheduled sampling (mix ground-truth and own predictions with a decaying probability)
papers: Scheduled Sampling for Sequence Prediction with Recurrent Neural Networks (Bengio, Vinyals, Jaitly, Shazeer, NeurIPS 2015) https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.03099 (read via ar5iv)
idea: Per token flip a coin: with probability eps_i feed the ground-truth previous token, else the model's own sample or argmax; eps_i decays over training (curriculum from easy to realistic).
formulation: schedules linear eps_i = max(eps, k - c i), exponential eps_i = k^i, inverse sigmoid eps_i = k/(k + exp(i/k)); the coin is per token (per sequence performed much worse); gradients are NOT propagated through the sampled token (left to future work); the term "exposure bias" is not used, the paper speaks of errors amplified early in the sequence. - input / output: RNN decoders.
training: regime `teacher_forcing` -> `free_rollout` curriculum.
differentiable: partial - no gradient through the sampled token.
sensors_data: MSCOCO captioning, WSJ constituency parsing, speech frame prediction.
results: captioning (BLEU-4 / METEOR / CIDEr): baseline 28.8 / 24.2 / 89.5, scheduled sampling 30.6 / 24.3 / 92.1, always sampling 11.2 / 15.7 / 49.7; parsing F1: baseline 86.54, scheduled sampling 88.08, always sampling invalid trees; speech: always sampling 34.6 / 35.8 frame error rate vs baseline 15.0 (next-step) / 46.0 (decoding).
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort S - ramp the share of own children (instead of GT-nearest children) fed to the next level from 0 to 1; pure free roll-out from the start is documented as poor in captioning and parsing.
compat_needs: a decoder that accepts either GT or own input at each level.
compat_conflicts: the sampled input carries no gradient.

name: Polygon-RNN++ (beam of candidate polygons ranked by a separately trained evaluator; RL against exposure bias)
papers: Efficient Interactive Annotation of Segmentation Datasets with Polygon-RNN++ (Acuna, Ling, Kar, Fidler, CVPR 2018) https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.09693 (read via ar5iv)
idea: A ConvLSTM predicts polygon vertices one by one as a classification over a 28 x 28 grid (plus an end token); cross-entropy pre-training, then self-critical RL on IoU so the decoder trains on its own samples; at inference K = 5 first-vertex candidates each run a beam, and an evaluator network (trained with MSE to predict the IoU of a polygon) picks the best.
formulation: teacher-forced training with a distance-transform-smoothed target (Manhattan distance truncated at 2); RL: reward = IoU of predicted and GT masks, baseline = reward of the greedy polygon, temperature 0.6; evaluator candidates sampled at temperature 0.3 for diversity, trained separately after RL converged; beam width B not stated for the main results (fast variant B = K = 1, 295 ms per object). - input / output: image crop -> polygon vertices.
training: regime `teacher_forcing` then `rl`; selection by a learned verifier.
differentiable: no for the RL path (reward); evaluator is a separate regressor.
results: cumulative ablation mean IoU: residual Polygon-RNN 62.16, + attention 65.43, + RL 67.17, + evaluator 70.21, + GGNN 71.38; evaluator with greedy sequences 69.72 vs beam search without evaluator 67.49.
compute: 295 ms per object for B = K = 1.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - a learned verifier (IoU predictor) to choose among beam candidates and RL against exposure bias are both used; RL is outside our "no argmax on the training path" rule.
compat_needs: IoU-like reward; evaluator network.
compat_conflicts: RL / sampling; two-stage training.

name: On-policy closed-loop training for multimodal prediction (execute one mode, detach across transitions)
papers: Rectify, Don't Regret: On-Policy Closed-Loop Training for Multimodal Trajectory Prediction (Yadav, Bohn, Meisen, arXiv 2603.23393, v2 Sept 2026) https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23393 (arXiv HTML read; code https://github.com/harshy105/CL-Traj). A companion paper (arXiv 2603.24155) is marked withdrawn and is not used.
idea: A multimodal predictor is rolled out in closed loop during training: each predicted mode is supervised only on states its own execution produced, and gradients are cut at the executed transitions so the model learns to recover from drift instead of "regretting" an earlier prediction.
formulation: receding horizon: each predicted mode is executed for T_sim (default 2.0 s, T_pred = 6 s), the model re-predicts from the resulting state; stop-gradient on the executed ego positions. The open-loop sample (n = 0) supervises classification (mode probabilities) and regression of all M modes; closed-loop samples (n >= 1) supervise only regression of the executed mode m*, with the original logged future as target; m* is chosen from the open-loop sample by L2 distance to the ground truth (WTA) and fixed for the rollout, so training unrolls ONE mode (cost scales with replanning count, not M x replanning). At test time all M modes are rolled out. An off-policy variant that re-selects the best mode each step was worse, especially at T_sim = 0.5 s. A fully differentiable closed loop ties the policy to the training replanning rate (shown in a figure only). - input / output: LMFormer-D (decoder-only) and an unmodified QCNet.
training: regime `free_rollout` (on-policy, detached) mixed with open-loop teacher signal; 5 seeds main, 3 ablations.
results: closed-loop evaluation at T_sim = 0.5 s, collision % open-loop -> closed-loop training: nuScenes 3.95 -> 3.08, DeepScenario 4.46 -> 2.92, Argoverse 2 (QCNet) 2.84 -> 2.35; off-road % 5.65 -> 1.86, 22.28 -> 8.62, 16.67 -> 15.07; at T_sim = 6.0 s the two are comparable; abstract: up to 35 % fewer collisions, 67 % fewer off-road.
compute: closed-loop samples add cost proportional to replanning frequency; LMFormer-D has 45 % fewer parameters and 62 % fewer FLOPs than LMFormer.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - the only direct evidence for free roll-out with multiple hypotheses: execute the GT-nearest hypothesis (WTA from the teacher sample), supervise regression only for it, keep the classification (score) signal from the teacher-forced sample, detach across levels.
compat_needs: a one-mode rollout path through the tree (the GT-nearest child continues), a separate teacher-forced pass for scores.
compat_conflicts: detaching cuts the path from the downstream loss to the early children (our E121 finding that planner gradients through positions give no gain fits).

name: Differentiable beam search for graph generation (decoding-aware training for information extraction)
papers: Information Extraction with Differentiable Beam Search on Graph RNNs (El Khbir, Tomeh, Charnois, LREC-COLING 2024) https://aclanthology.org/2024.lrec-main.796/ (abstract only)
idea: Graph generation cast as autoregressive sequence labelling; training is made decoding-aware with a differentiable version of beam search to reduce exposure bias; a new way to quantify exposure bias is proposed.
formulation: not read (the page does not say which relaxation or loss). - input / output: not read.
training: decoding-aware; regime `free_rollout`.
results: gains over a version without decoding-aware training (abstract); numbers not seen.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - recent evidence that differentiable-beam training is used for graph-structured outputs, but only in text.
compat_needs: not read.
compat_conflicts: not read.

name: Trexplorer Super (recurrent DETR tracking of tree centrelines; super-trajectory training; duplicate branches)
papers: Trexplorer Super (Naeem et al., MICCAI 2025, arXiv 2507.10881; full title not on the page read) https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.10881 (arXiv HTML read); the original Trexplorer: Recurrent DETR for Topologically Correct Tree Centerline Tracking (MICCAI 2024; PDF not decodable); RefTr: Recurrent Refinement of Confluent Trajectories for 3D Vascular Tree Centerlines (Naeem et al., arXiv 2511.20823) https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20823 (abstract only)
idea: A DETR decoder tracks each branch breadth-first, predicting the child nodes of the next graph level (end / intermediate / bifurcation); patches are placed at the endpoints of the graph built so far and the query outputs of the previous patch are carried over. Known problems of the first version: duplicate branches and premature termination.
formulation: Hungarian loss between predicted and GT nodes with self-attention among queries to suppress duplicates (individual loss terms not specified); history = past-trajectory token of up to 10 previous node positions; Super Trajectory Training: a sample is a super trajectory of 54 nodes split into six sub-trajectories of 10 nodes with shared link nodes, query outputs passed between them (so the model trains on its own carried state, not only GT); target augmentation samples Laplace offsets at bifurcations (scale proportional to radius) to create more bifurcation targets; Focal Cross Attention (high-resolution features, attention restricted to a focal region around the tracked branch); inference: 26 queries assigned at a bifurcation, some discarded, at most 196 tokens tracked concurrently, no NMS, no post-processing. The page does not describe teacher forcing or multi-hypothesis methods. - input / output: 3-D image patches -> tree nodes.
training: regime `hungarian_set` per step; STT gives a form of free rollout inside super trajectories.
differentiable: partial - Hungarian assignment; carried queries are differentiable.
results: point F1 (Vesselformer / Trexplorer / Trexplorer Super): synthetic 48.18 / 39.40 / 77.83; ATM'22 26.77 / 3.34 / 60.45; Parse 2022 16.43 / 10.01 / 39.46; branch F1 15.95 / 26.26 / 77.12 (synthetic), 1.95 / 3.34 / 41.15 (ATM'22); Betti errors zero for both Trexplorer variants.
code: https://github.com/RomStriker/Trexplorer-Super (paper CC BY-NC-ND 4.0; code licence not stated on the page)
fit_to_us: baseline - effort L - closest published tree tracker with several children per step; shows duplicates and early stops as the failure modes of the matched version, and training on carried (own) state as the fix.
compat_needs: Hungarian; 3-D patches.
compat_conflicts: Hungarian; patch-based inputs.

name: Modified multiple hypothesis tracking for tree extraction (ranked local hypotheses, search-depth tree)
papers: Extracting Tree-structures in CT data by Tracking Multiple Statistically Ranked Hypotheses (Selvan et al.) https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.08981 (read via ar5iv)
idea: Classical hypothesis-tree tracking: at regularly spaced steps tubular templates are fitted in a few directions, local hypotheses are ranked, and a tree of depth d of hypotheses is built; decisions are deferred until a branch scores well across several steps.
formulation: step length = scaled local radius; search angle 70 degrees with 2 angles for airways; template profile steepness 8, weighted least squares; score = 1 / rank among the N hypotheses at that step (best = 1, removes scale dependence); global hypothesis = d local hypotheses scored by the average rank score; bifurcations: spectral clustering of hypotheses; tree state saved and tracking resumed per new branch; global threshold 0.7 (airways); search depth 6 (airways), 4 (coronary); after a decision, hypotheses that are not children of the best node are discarded. - input / output: CT volume intensities (or probability images) -> centreline tree.
training: none (classical); parameter tuning at depth 6 took about 88 hours.
sensors_data: airway CT (16 test scans), coronary CT.
results: mean centreline error 1.93 mm vs 3.96 mm original MHT, 3.37 mm region growing on intensity, 2.06 mm region growing on probability images (p = 0.1 vs the last); coronary overlap 91.8 % vs 67.6 % original MHT; about 15 s per airway scan, 3 s per vessel.
compute: depth 4 - 6 feasible, trade-off between under-segmentation and run time.
fit_to_us: baseline - effort M - the non-learned counterpart of our tree: local template sampling, rank-based scores, deferred decision by depth; rank scores 1/R are a calibration-free alternative to raw validity.
compat_needs: local scores per hypothesis.
compat_conflicts: not trainable.

name: DTPP / TPP (pre-generated ego trajectory tree, conditional prediction, learned cost, joint differentiable training)
papers: DTPP: Differentiable Joint Conditional Prediction and Cost Evaluation for Tree Policy Planning in Autonomous Driving (Huang, Karkus, Ivanovic, Chen, Pavone, Lv, ICRA 2024) https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05885 (arXiv HTML read); Tree-structured Policy Planning with Learned Behavior Models (Chen, Karkus, Ivanovic, Weng, Pavone, 2023) https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.11902 (abstract level)
idea: The ego tree of candidate trajectories is PRE-GENERATED (lane-centric target sampling), a conditional prediction model decodes all branches in one pass, a learned cost scores each branch, and prediction and cost are trained jointly; pruning to the top nodes halves the run time.
formulation: tree: two stages (0 - 3 s, 3 - 8 s); stage 1 from three reference paths with up to 30 sampled target states (third-order polynomial speed profiles), keep the top 5 nodes, expand each with 6 targets for stage 2; infeasible trajectories dropped, random discarding above the node limit M = 30. Cost per branch = horizon-averaged weighted sum of ego features, learned interaction features and a Gaussian RBF collision feature, weights from an MLP on the ego encoding (10 weights); P(s_m) = softmax(-c). Loss: smooth L1 for the prediction on the branch closest to the GT ego trajectory + cross-entropy of softmax-normalised plan scores against the GT label; weights beta1 = 1.0, beta2 = 0.2, IRL alpha = 0.1; the cost loss back-propagates into the prediction module; gradient through the branch selection not stated. - input / output: 10 agents, ego, 50 map elements (transformer, D = 256, 3 layers) -> branch trajectories, costs.
training: nuPlan, RTX 3080, batch 16, 20 epochs; regime `matching_free` (nearest branch as label).
differentiable: partial - candidate generation and pruning are rule-based; cost and prediction are differentiable.
results: NR / R score: DTPP 0.8964 / 0.8978 (collision 0.025), TPP 0.7388 / 0.7699, PDM 0.9061 / 0.9150, IDM 0.6396 / 0.6168; tree vs single stage: single-3 s 0.7087 / 0.7044, single-8 s 0.7799 / 0.7558; joint vs separate training (no pruning) 0.8948 / 0.8933 vs 0.8134 / 0.8106.
compute: 98.0 ms with pruning vs 199.6 ms without.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - the nearest published "pre-generated hypothesis tree + learned scoring + nearest-branch label + joint differentiable training"; pruning the top nodes per stage with a rule is accepted practice.
compat_needs: a candidate generator; a nearest-branch label; a node-wise cost.
compat_conflicts: the tree is not learned (rule-based), nodes are ego trajectories, not map elements.

name: Multiple hypothesis tracking with learned parts (online appearance models; neural gating of the hypothesis tree)
papers: Multiple Hypothesis Tracking Revisited (Kim, Li, Ciptadi, Rehg, ICCV 2015) https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_iccv_2015/html/Kim_Multiple_Hypothesis_Tracking_ICCV_2015_paper.html (PDF returned 403, listing and search summary only); Multi-object Tracking with Neural Gating Using Bilinear LSTM (Kim, Li, Rehg, ECCV 2018) https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content_ECCV_2018/html/Chanho_Kim_Multi-object_Tracking_with_ECCV_2018_paper.html (abstract and survey summary only)
idea: Track-oriented MHT keeps a tree of association hypotheses per track and prunes it; Kim 2015 adds online-trained regularised-least-squares appearance models per hypothesis branch; Kim 2018 uses a bilinear LSTM whose affinity score gates (prunes) branches of the hypothesis tree and scores tracks by appearance and motion.
formulation: not read. - input / output: detections per frame -> tracks.
training: Kim 2018: LSTM trained on tracklet appearance features; the tree itself is not trained.
differentiable: no for the tree (gating network yes).
results: state-of-the-art near-online performance on MOT16 / MOT17 (abstract); numbers not seen. Searches for a learned or differentiable MHT with trainable hypothesis tree found none; transformer trackers (TrackFormer, MOTR, TADN) are not hypothesis trees.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - confirms the pattern "learned gate decides which branch of a hypothesis tree survives" without end-to-end training of the tree.
compat_needs: not read.
compat_conflicts: not read.

name: Online Navigation Refinement (MAT on OMA): SD roads to perceived centre-lines, route attribution after perception
papers: Online Navigation Refinement: Achieving Lane-Level Guidance by Associating Standard-Definition and Online Perception Maps (authors not read; repo owner WallelWan; ICLR 2026 per repo README) https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.07487
idea: Input is an SD road graph (OSM; each road an ordered sequence of directed vectors with connectivity) and an online-perception (OP) map (lane centre-lines sampled uniformly with topology, plus boundary vectors) produced by MapTR / MapTRv2 / SeqGrowGraph at test time. A transformer assigns each perceived centre-line to exactly one SD road; an SD path (the route) then maps to a path of OP centre-lines by topological sorting. This is route attribution after perception, but hard and road-level, not a route probability per vertex.
formulation: tokens = vectors [x1, y1, x2, y2, theta] -> 2-layer MLP. Block = Path-Aware Attention (enumerate valid root-to-leaf paths, reorder tokens by path index, grouped attention over adjacent tokens, restore, average over paths) + Spatial Attention (3-D grid x, y, orientation, Hilbert-curve serialisation, grouped attention) + FFN. Head: Prob_ij = softmax over roads j of (feature of centre-line i . mean-pooled road feature j / sqrt d), not Sinkhorn. Post-processing: start at the most confident centre-line, bidirectional beam search constrained by road connectivity. Channels [96, 192, 384, 768, 1536]; blocks MAT-T [2,2,2,2,2], MAT-L [4,4,4,12,4].
input: SD road graph (vectors + connectivity) and OP centre-lines + boundaries in the ego frame; GPS pose is not an input (drift is treated as spatial noise).
output: per-centre-line road id (unique; a road may own several centre-lines); the route is the SD path mapped to an OP path by topological sorting.
training: loss 1.0 CE + 0.01 CTC on hand-annotated associations; dataset OMA built on nuScenes + OSM: over 30 K scenarios, 480 K road paths, 2.6 M lane vectors; train + val 31,724 (GT OP maps), test 5,573 (MapTRv2-generated OP maps), area-disjoint split; 50 epochs AdamW lr 1e-4, batch 128; regime: supervised.
differentiable: partial - the softmax head is differentiable; path extraction (beam search) is not; trained apart from the OP generator, no gradient into it.
sensors_data: nuScenes (Boston, Singapore) + OSM; OP maps come from camera BEV models; no radar.
results: val NR-F1(50:95) MAT-T 78.2, MAT-L 78.7, best baseline 72.9 (EAM3); test with OP maps from MapTR / MapTRv2 / SeqGrowGraph: MAT-L 41.9 / 45.0 / 54.9 vs EAM3 36.3 / 39.1 / 50.8. Imperfect SD maps (appendix, val / test): global shift 10 / 20 / 50 %: 77.5 / 43.3, 76.0 / 42.9, 74.6 / 41.4; element absence up to 30 %: 75.5 / 43.1. Zero-shot nuScenes-C hard: rain 40.6, fog 42.1, dark 41.6. Ablation val: path-aware attention alone 74.1 vs 61.8 plain backbone.
compute: latency 34 ms (T), 70 ms (L) on an A6000; parameters not stated.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - their SD input is road vectors, ours is SD raster tokens, and the association is hard and road-level.
compat_needs: OP lane graph as polylines with topology (our assembled graph); SD roads as vectors with connectivity; ego-frame alignment within GPS-level drift.
compat_conflicts: hard unique assignment vs our soft route probability; beam-search post-processing not differentiable; trained on GT OP maps, tested on generated ones; separate from perception (no end-to-end).
tried_before: E102-E104 (route attribution inside the learned chain; cross-attention kept, route success 0.853-0.820) is the end-to-end analogue; vector-SD association not tried.

name: PDM-Closed / PDM-Open / PDM-Hybrid (rule-based centre-line planner, closed-loop test bed)
papers: Parting with Misconceptions about Learning-based Vehicle Motion Planning (Dauner, Hallgarten, Geiger, Chitta; CoRL 2023) https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.07962
idea: nuPlan planner that needs only the route's centre-line, forecasts of other agents and the drivable-area map for scoring: IDM proposals along the centre-line, rolled out by an LQR tracker on a kinematic bicycle model, best chosen by a nuPlan-like proxy score. PDM-Open (MLP on centre-line + ego history) reaches the best open-loop score without agent or map input beyond the centre-line; PDM-Hybrid adds a learned offset. Core message: open-loop and closed-loop scores are misaligned.
formulation: centre-line from a graph search over the lanes of the route (algorithm name not confirmed on the pages read). Route = roadblock-id sequence, repaired in code by BFS (start off-route: backward depth 15, else forward depth 30; gaps between consecutive roadblocks bridged by forward BFS depth 30; loops cut). Proposals: 5 target speeds (20 ... 100 % of the speed limit) x 3 lateral offsets (-1, 0, +1 m) = 15, 4 s at 10 Hz; others forecast with constant velocity over 8 s; best proposal extended to 8 s by IDM; emergency brake if a collision is expected within 2 s; score weights in the supplement (not read). PDM-Open: centre-line at 1 m up to 120 m + 2 s ego history at 5 Hz, each projected to 512, MLP 2 x 512, 8 s output at 0.5 s.
input: ego pose, lane graph (nuPlan map API), route roadblock ids, tracked objects, drivable-area map (scorer).
training: none for Closed; L1 imitation on about 177 k scenarios for Open / Hybrid.
sensors_data: nuPlan with privileged GT map and GT objects (paper: localisation errors, map imperfections, misdetections are not considered); Val14 = 1,118 scenarios.
results: Val14 CLS-R / CLS-NR / OLS: PDM-Closed 92 / 93 / 42; PDM-Hybrid 92 / 93 / 84; PDM-Open 54 / 50 / 86; IDM 77 / 76 / 38; GC-PGP (lane-graph GNN planner) 55 / 59 / 83; Urban Driver 50 / 53 / 82; PlanCNN 72 / 73 / 64; log replay 80 / 94 / 100. 2023 nuPlan challenge: PDM-Hybrid 90, rank 1 of 25.
compute: PDM-Closed 91 ms, PDM-Open 7 ms, PDM-Hybrid 96 ms (hardware not stated).
fit_to_us: reimplement - effort M - the original needs nuPlan devkit and nuPlan maps; the principle (best route path through the graph by dynamic programming over route probability, IDM, proxy score) is small.
compat_needs: lane graph with successors; route (roadblock ids or our per-vertex route probability); drivable-area raster; centre-line at 1 m up to about 120 m (our BEV reaches 50 m forward); speed limit.
compat_conflicts: privileged-map assumption; the roadblock BFS repair has no counterpart for a predicted graph with gaps; centre-line quality is the single point of failure.
tried_before: none (E117 is a learned consumer; no rule-based consumer in the project).

name: PlanTF (polygon tokens with on-route flag, state-dropout encoder)
papers: Rethinking Imitation-based Planner for Autonomous Driving (Cheng et al., ICRA 2024) https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10443 ; project page https://jchengai.github.io/planTF
depth: M (partial: the HTML extraction lacked the map section) + C
idea: Transformer encoder (adapted from a masked-autoencoder forecasting model) over agent and map tokens; the ego plan is decoded from the ego token. Shows that kinematic ego state / history gives a shortcut: strong open-loop score, weak closed-loop score. Fixes: position-only ego input, state dropout encoder (SDE), perturbation augmentation with re-normalisation.
formulation: map input (from code): polygons = lanes + lane connectors + crosswalks within a +-100 m square (no cap in the builder; padded to the longest sample in the batch). Per polygon three polylines (centre, left, right) x 20 points (21 sampled, last dropped). The released encoder uses ONLY the centre polyline: per point [p - polygon_center (2, translation only), vector to next point (2), cos / sin heading (2)] = 6 channels -> point encoder (`PointsEncoder`, internals not read) -> 128-d; added embeddings: polygon type (3), on_route (2, roadblock-id membership), traffic-light status (4, UNKNOWN allowed), speed limit by MLP or learned "unknown" embedding. Positional embedding from (x, y, cos, sin) of the polygon centre. Ego frame at the current pose. Key padding: polygon masked if no valid point; point validity = inside the square. No adjacency; no map augmentation found. Agents: 2 s history, up to 64. Depth 4, dim 128, 8 heads, drop-path 0.2, 6 modes, 80 future steps (8 s), SDE dropout 0.75.
input: polygon feature dict (above) + agent histories.
output: 6 trajectories with probabilities + predictions of other agents.
training: imitation (loss terms not found on the page); ego-state perturbation with probability 0.5; 25 epochs, batch 128, lr 1e-3 cosine, weight decay 1e-4, at most 1 M frames; regime: teacher forcing / imitation.
differentiable: yes for the network; the map is GT, no gradient to a map head.
sensors_data: nuPlan, GT map + GT tracked objects; radius 100 m.
results: Test14-random OLS 87.07 / NR-CLS 86.48 / R-CLS 80.59; Test14-hard 83.32 / 72.68 / 61.70; Val14 (own Table VII) 89.18 / 84.83 / 76.78 (PLUTO's table lists PlanTF at 85.30 / 77.07 on Val14: differs between papers). SDE dropout 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.75 on Test14-random: NR-CLS 81.70 / 83.71 / 86.48 while OLS falls 89.11 / 89.12 / 87.07.
compute: cache of 1 M frames "20+ hours"; 4-6 GB GPU memory per GPU at batch 32 (README); parameters not stated.
fit_to_us: adapt_code - effort M - requires nuPlan devkit and Python 3.9, but the feature dict is a clean contract to emit from our graph.
compat_needs: polygons with 20 centre points, polygon centre, on_route flag, per-point valid mask, ego-frame coordinates.
compat_conflicts: no connectivity input (topology only implicit); range 100 m vs our 50 m; route flag is roadblock-level (coarser than our lane-level route); ego motion as input causes the copycat shortcut (E117 uses ego motion).
tried_before: none for polygon consumers; E117 is the own consumer.

name: PLUTO (route-restricted reference lines as lateral queries, contrastive negatives)
papers: PLUTO: Pushing the Limit of Imitation Learning-based Planning for Autonomous Driving (Cheng, Chen, Chen; 2024) https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.14327
idea: One trajectory per (reference line x longitudinal query). Reference lines come from the lane graph and the route; the 12 longitudinal queries are learned embeddings. An auxiliary drivable-area loss and a contrastive imitation loss with positive / negative scene augmentations are added; a reference-free head covers scenes without a reference line.
formulation: map polylines with 8 channels per point (p_i - p_0, p_i - p_{i-1}, p_i - p_left, p_i - p_right), PointNet encoder; speed limit and traffic-light status as attribute embeddings; Fourier embedding of global position. Reference lines (code, RouteManager): start lanes within 3 m of the ego on a route roadblock with heading error below 90 deg; depth-first search over `outgoing_edges` restricted to route roadblocks, stop at 15 lanes or 100 m; trim from the ego projection; drop paths shorter than 0.8 x length; de-duplicate when the maximum coordinate difference is below 0.5 m; feature = 100 points per line (every 4th sample) + future projection of the ego. Decoder: lateral queries (reference lines) x N_L = 12 longitudinal queries, D = 128, 4 + 4 layers; output 80 steps x 6 channels; top K = 20 of N_R x N_L modes. Loss = L_i (smooth-L1 on the target query selected by teacher forcing from the GT endpoint + CE on mode scores) + L_p + L_aux (hinge on an ESDF cost map 500 x 500 at 0.2 m, 3 covering circles) + L_c (softmax triplet, temperature 0.1), all weights 1. Positive augmentation: ego-state perturbation, dropout of non-interactive agents; negative: remove leading agent, insert a leading agent from another sample, remove interactive agent, invert traffic lights; batch tripled. Model code (pluto_model.py): defaults dim 128, 4 encoder + 4 decoder layers, 8 heads, 6 modes, drop-path 0.2, dropout 0.1, `use_ego_history=False`, state dropout 0.75, `ref_free_traj=False` (the reference-free head is optional; the evaluation fallback for scenes without reference line needs it enabled); the map encoder uses lane boundaries (`use_lane_boundary=True`); position embedding = Fourier embedding of (x, y, heading) of agents and polygon centres; key padding from the validity masks of agents, polygons and static objects; the reference-line validity only masks the output probabilities at evaluation.
input: map polylines, agents (20 steps), static obstacles, reference lines.
training: loss above; 1 M frames, 25 epochs, batch 128, AdamW; regime: imitation with teacher-forced reference-line choice + contrastive.
differentiable: yes for the network; reference-line generation is a rule (DFS), no gradient to the map.
results: Val14 non-reactive / reactive score: PLUTO with post-processing 93.21 / 92.06, without 89.04 / 80.01; PDM-Closed 93.08 / 93.20; PlanTF 85.30 / 77.07; PlanTF-H 89.96 / 88.08; GameFormer 82.95 / 83.88; log replay 93.68 / 81.24.
compute: 4 x RTX 3090, about 45 h with the contrastive loss (22 h without); parameters not stated.
code: https://github.com/jchengai/pluto (README: training part not fully tested)
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - DFS over route-filtered successors is exactly what our edge graph + route probability supports; the reference-free head is a model for the "no usable lane" case.
compat_needs: successor edges, a route filter, polylines resampled to a fixed point count, drivable-area raster for the auxiliary loss.
compat_conflicts: roadblock-level route; nuPlan devkit; DFS on a graph with false forks multiplies reference lines (only the 0.5 m de-duplication limits their number).

name: Diffusion Planner (lane tensor 70 x 20 x 12, route lanes through adaLN)
papers: Diffusion-based Planning for Autonomous Driving with Flexible Guidance (Zheng et al., ICLR 2025) https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15564
idea: A DiT-style transformer denoises the joint future of the ego and 10 neighbours conditioned on scene tokens; route lanes condition every block via adaptive layer norm; inference-time classifier guidance with energy functions (collision, speed range, comfort, drivable area).
formulation: lanes (code map_process.py): 70 x 20 points x 12 channels [centre xy (2), vector to next centre point (2), left-boundary offset (2), right-boundary offset (2), traffic-light one-hot (4)]; speed limit and has-speed-limit stored per lane (70 x 1). Lanes = LANE + LANE_CONNECTOR within a radius, ranked by minimum distance of any centre point to the ego, nearest kept; successors NOT traversed; linear resampling to the fixed point count; empty slots zero-filled with an `avails` mask. Route lanes: 25 (Table 5) with the shared max_points (20) built by the same routine (paper: coordinates only), from route roadblock ids pruned by connectivity. Ego-centric, then z-score x (mu 10, sigma 20), y scaled by sigma 20. Neighbours 32 x 21 steps x 11 features (predicts 10). MLP-Mixer encoders; hidden 192, 3 encoder + 3 decoder blocks, 6 heads. Route embedding is added to the timestep embedding and applied via adaLN to all tokens. VP linear schedule (beta 0.1 ... 20), x0-prediction MSE, DPM-Solver++ 10 steps, temperature 0.5 (0.1 with refinement). Drivable-area energy = signed-distance cost map of the lanes; route not used in guidance. Encoder code (encoder.py): validity is read from all-zero rows, not from `avails` (a lane whose points all have zero geometry is masked through key_padding_mask; padding points inside a valid lane still enter the mean pooling); lane token = MLP-Mixer over the 20 points (token dim 64, channels 128) mean-pooled to 128-d, plus speed-limit Linear(1 -> 128) or a learned unknown embedding, plus traffic-light Linear(4 -> 128) taken from the first point of the lane; positional embedding Linear(7 -> hidden) of (x, y, cos, sin) + 3-way token-type one-hot; tokens concatenated [neighbours, static objects, lanes] and processed by plain self-attention blocks (no cross-attention); encoder.py has no separate route input (route handling sits in the decoder; code not read).
input: ego state, neighbours, static objects, lanes, route lanes.
output: joint ego + neighbour trajectories, 8 s at 10 Hz.
training: x0-prediction MSE; about 11 M sampled nuPlan scenarios, 500 epochs, batch 2048, lr 5e-4; ego-state perturbation + quintic interpolation to the GT future; regime: denoising.
differentiable: yes (network); guidance differentiates energies w.r.t. the sample, not the map.
sensors_data: nuPlan GT map; delivery-vehicle data (about 200 h) as a second source.
results: closed-loop non-reactive / reactive: Val14 89.87 / 82.80, Test14-hard 75.99 / 69.22, Test14 89.19 / 82.93; with refinement Val14 94.26 / 92.90, Test14-hard 78.87 / 82.00; delivery data 92.08.
compute: about 20 Hz on one A6000 (appendix); training 8 x A100 80 GB; parameters not stated.
fit_to_us: adapt_code - effort M - the lane tensor contract is useful, but boundary offsets and traffic-light channels do not exist in our graph.
compat_needs: fixed-size lane tensor in which invalid lanes are all-zero rows (the encoder derives its mask from zero geometry), ordered route lanes, ego-frame coordinates.
compat_conflicts: no edges used; boundaries and traffic lights must be zero / unknown; 100 m vs 50 m range; trained only on the nuPlan distribution.

name: GameFormer (level-k interactive prediction + planning) and GameFormer-Planner code
papers: GameFormer: Game-theoretic Modeling and Learning of Transformer-based Interactive Prediction and Planning (Huang et al., ICCV 2023) https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.05760
idea: Level-0 decoder predicts every agent from scene context; level k re-conditions each agent's decoder on the level k-1 futures of all other agents. The nuPlan pipeline adds reference-path selection from the route and a differentiable Gauss-Newton refinement.
formulation: prediction model: agent history 11 steps (1 s), 22 agents; map up to 6 drivable lanes per target agent x 100 waypoints x 15 features (centre, left, right position and heading, speed limit, lane type, traffic light, stop-sign control), up to 4 crosswalks x 100 x 3, max-pooled to 60 lane + 20 crosswalk tokens; D = 256; K = 6 levels (K = 4 for open-loop planning). Route (paper): reference path from a cubic spline through traversed-lane waypoints, 100 m ahead, 1000 points at 0.1 m, 5 channels. Code (GameFormer-Planner): lanes (N, P, 3) = x, y, heading (+ 4 traffic-light one-hot = 7), route_lanes (N, P, 3) from route roadblock ids, crosswalks (N, P, 3); nearest N by minimum point distance; boundaries computed but not returned; `avails` (N, P) mask; ego frame at the present state; no other normalisation; N, P from config (not seen). Loss = L_IL (NLL of best mode per step + CE, every level) + 0.1 L_Inter (repulsive potential). Refinement: DIPP-style Gauss-Newton (max 30 iterations, step 0.3), cost weights learned through the optimiser.
input: ego / agent histories, lanes, route, crosswalks.
output: M joint trajectories (GMM) per level + refined ego plan.
training: planning 20 epochs, AdamW lr 1e-4, batch 32, one RTX 3080; regime: imitation + interaction loss.
results: nuPlan test benchmark overall 0.8288 (OL 0.8400, CL-NR 0.8087, CL-R 0.8376; second behind 0.8745); Waymo interactive (J, M = 6) minADE 0.9161, minFDE 1.9373, MR 0.4531, mAP 0.1376; WOMD closed loop success 73.16 % -> 94.50 % with refinement.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - reference path from the route plus differentiable refinement could post-process E117's path; the level-k part needs agents, which we do not predict.
compat_needs: route lanes, lane centre-lines with heading, mask.
compat_conflicts: no connectivity; needs agents for the game part; nuPlan devkit.

name: DTPP (tree policy planning with learned cost)
papers: DTPP: Differentiable Joint Conditional Prediction and Cost Evaluation for Tree Policy Planning (Huang et al., ICRA 2024) https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05885
idea: Ego plans a two-stage tree of candidate trajectories along reference paths; a query-centric transformer predicts all agents conditioned on every branch in one pass; a context-aware learned cost scores branches; softmax over costs + cross-entropy trains cost and prediction jointly.
formulation: 3 reference paths (lane centre-lines from map and route, as in GameFormer); stage 1 (0-3 s) up to 30 target states over the paths, top 5 kept by learned cost; stage 2 (3-8 s) 6 targets per node, up to 30 branches; third-order polynomial speed profile; dynamic programming selects the first action. Encoder: 10 agents + ego, 20 past steps, 50 nearest map elements (lanes + crosswalks, MLP, dim 256, points per lane not stated), 3 self-attention layers; decoder with multi-axis (time / mode) causal attention. Cost = time-averaged weighted sum of ego features (jerk, acceleration, speed, lateral acceleration), a learned 5-d interaction feature and a Gaussian-RBF collision feature; weights from a 10-d MLP on the ego encoding. Loss = sum over stages beta^j (L_p smooth-L1 on the branch closest to the GT plan + 0.1 L_c cross-entropy), beta = 1.0, 0.2.
input: lane graph (50 elements), route reference paths, agent histories.
output: selected ego trajectory + predicted agent futures per branch.
training: 100 k scenarios from the nuPlan validation split, 20 epochs, batch 16, AdamW lr 1e-4, one RTX 3080; regime: imitation / max-entropy IRL form.
differentiable: yes (costs are differentiable functions of predicted states; softmax selection in training).
sensors_data: nuPlan GT; 200 test scenarios (20 per type).
results: nuPlan closed-loop non-reactive / reactive: DTPP 0.8964 / 0.8978; PDM 0.9061 / 0.9150; IDM 0.6396 / 0.6168; TPP 0.7388 / 0.7699; open-loop 0.7911.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - a tree of route-conditioned candidates scored by a learned cost parallels our hypothesis-tree thinking on the planner side.
compat_needs: reference paths from lane graph + route; map elements as tokens.
compat_conflicts: needs agent futures; nuPlan devkit.

name: VAD (map vectors as planner input and planning constraints; gradient into map points)
papers: VAD: Vectorized Scene Representation for Efficient Autonomous Driving (Jiang et al., ICCV 2023) https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12077
idea: Map queries predict 100 polylines x 20 points in 3 classes (lane divider, pedestrian crossing, road boundary). The ego query attends agent queries, then map queries (separate positional encoders); an MLP on [ego feature after agent attention, after map attention, ego status, command] outputs the plan. Training-only planning constraints use the predicted vectors.
formulation: ego-boundary hinge L_bd = max(0, delta_bd - d), d = distance of each waypoint to the nearest predicted boundary point, delta_bd = 1.0 m; ego-lane direction L_dir = angular difference between the ego step vector and the nearest lane-divider vector within 2.0 m; collision hinge with delta_X 1.5 m, delta_Y 3.0 m. Only predicted instances with class score >= 0.5 enter. Config weights: bound 1.0, direction 0.5, collision 1.0, regression 1.0; map cls focal 2.0, points L1 1.0, direction cosine 0.005; BEV 200 x 200 over 30 x 60 m; 4-frame queue; 3 discrete commands. Code: min over all map points of the Euclidean distance (gradient reaches the selected point); atan2 of gathered points for the yaw term (gradient reaches map points); scores only act as boolean masks (no gradient); `perception_detach` exists in the bound loss, default False, not set in the config.
input: multi-view BEV features, ego status (CAN bus), command.
output: 6-step ego trajectory + map vectors + agent motion.
training: map and agent losses of its own heads (matching as in MapTR, from memory) + planning losses; fully end-to-end.
differentiable: partial - planning gradients reach predicted map point coordinates; class scores get none; matching and thresholds are discrete.
results: nuScenes val avg L2 / collision: VAD-Base 0.72 m / 0.22 %, VAD-Tiny 0.78 / 0.38, UniAD 1.03 / 0.31. Ablation (Table 2): full 0.72 / 0.22; no map interaction 0.86 / 0.29; no agent interaction 0.82 / 0.26; no constraints 0.76 / 0.28; only overstep 0.80 / 0.24; only direction 0.75 / 0.25. Rasterised vs vectorised map 0.74 / 0.39 vs 0.72 / 0.22.
compute: VAD-Tiny 59.5 ms (16.8 FPS), VAD-Base 224.3 ms (4.5 FPS) on an RTX 3090.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort S - hinge constraints on the nearest vertex / edge (1.0 m, 2.0 m, confidence 0.5) are easy; the boundary term needs road boundaries, which a centre-line graph lacks.
compat_needs: ordered map points with a class score; an ego trajectory head.
compat_conflicts: Hungarian matching in the original map head; mmcv / mmdet3d stack; ego-status leakage on nuScenes open loop.
tried_before: E121 (planner loss through the positions: no gain) is the same idea; VAD's own gain from the constraints is small (L2 0.76 -> 0.72).

name: UncAD (per-vertex Laplace uncertainty into planning and trajectory selection)
papers: UncAD: Towards Safe End-to-end Autonomous Driving via Online Map Uncertainty (Yang et al., ICRA 2025) https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.12826
idea: Every predicted map point carries a Laplace scale; the scales are encoded into "uncertainty queries", concatenated with the map queries and used as keys / values for agent and ego attention; at inference candidate trajectories are scored against the Laplace ellipses of boundary points and risky ones are set to zero.
formulation: map head output V_m of shape N_v x N_p x 4 (N_v = 100, N_p = 20; mu x, y and scale b x, y); loss = Laplace NLL, sum over points of log(2b) + |p - mu| / b; Q_unc = MLP(b); Q_m' = MLP([Q_m, Q_unc]) is the key / value of the agent and ego cross-attention; planner output 3 commands x N modes with confidences; UCAS: filter by command, score each trajectory point by NLL against the boundary ellipses, set the score to 0 if risk is high (threshold not stated), plus the base collision check and L2 distance to boundaries; the best remaining trajectory is output. Total loss = lambda_1 L_map (NLL) + lambda_2 L_mot + lambda_3 L_plan (weights not given).
input: VAD- or SparseDrive-style map instances with scales.
training: end-to-end, no extra uncertainty label; 8 x RTX 3090; epochs not given.
differentiable: partial - uncertainty enters as features (differentiable); trajectory selection is a hard filter.
results: nuScenes L2 / collision / drivable-area conflict rate DACR (a frame counts if any of the 4 ego corners lies outside the drivable area): VAD 0.72 / 0.23 % / 1.39 %; VAD + UncAD 0.62 / 0.17 % / 0.80 %; SparseDrive 0.61 / 0.10 / 1.06; SparseDrive + UncAD 0.60 / 0.07 / 0.88. Abstract: up to 26 % fewer collisions, up to 42 % fewer drivable-area conflicts, +1.9 % parameters.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort S - our validity / keep probability is the analogue of 1 / b; there is no per-vertex position scale yet.
compat_needs: per-vertex uncertainty in the same tensor as the positions; a candidate-trajectory scorer.
compat_conflicts: thresholds unspecified; selection is non-differentiable.
tried_before: none (E120 refinement and the keep gate exist, but not as planner input).

name: SparseDrive (sparse map instances as planner keys / values)
papers: SparseDrive: End-to-End Autonomous Driving via Sparse Scene Representation (Sun et al., ICRA 2025) https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19620
idea: Symmetric sparse perception (detection / tracking and online mapping share one decoder design) feeds a parallel motion planner. Map instances: N_m = 100 polylines x N_p = 20 points with anchors from K-means. The ego instance (initialised from the pooled smallest-scale front-camera feature) attends agents and map instances and plans in command-specific modes (K_p = 6, T_p = 6). Hierarchical selection: command filter, then collision-aware rescoring with the two most confident agent trajectories.
formulation: ego anchor from kinematics, velocity from the previous prediction (against ego-status leakage); ego status decoded as an auxiliary output; agent-temporal cross-attention, agent-agent self-attention, agent-map cross-attention; memory queue of 3 frames; mapping range 60 x 30 m; tracking id once confidence exceeds 0.2.
input: multi-view image features.
output: ego trajectories per command + scores; map and agent instances.
training: stage 1 perception from scratch (S: 100 epochs batch 8 lr 4e-4; B: 80 epochs), stage 2 joint 10 epochs with no frozen weights (no detach mentioned); regime: Hungarian matching for instances (from memory), imitation for planning.
differentiable: partial - stage-2 gradients reach perception queries; instance matching, top-k and rescoring are discrete.
results: nuScenes val avg L2 / collision: SparseDrive-S 0.61 m / 0.08 %, -B 0.58 / 0.06 (VAD-style metrics); UniAD 0.73 / 0.61 and VAD 0.72 / 0.21 in the same table; collision-aware rescoring 0.12 -> 0.08 %; no ablation on map features or ego status.
compute: 9.0 FPS (S), 7.3 FPS (B) on an RTX 4090; 85.9 M / 104.7 M parameters; training 18 + 2 h (S).
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort M - instance features + anchors as keys / values and per-command modes are portable, the mmcv-based code is not.
compat_needs: map instance tensor (feature + 20 x 2 anchors) and detections for the rescoring.
compat_conflicts: Hungarian matching; mmdet3d stack; K-means anchors over polylines assume a fixed point order.
tried_before: E31 / E32 (matched sparse set decoder dropped) concern the perception side only.

name: UniAD (planner reads BEV + ego query; map queries reach it only through MotionFormer)
papers: Planning-oriented Autonomous Driving (Hu et al., CVPR 2023) https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.10156
depth: M (tail of the page not read)
idea: MapFormer produces map queries (300 thing queries for lanes / dividers / crossings with Hungarian matching + 1 stuff query for the drivable area) and a panoptic map; only the map queries go on to MotionFormer, where agent and map queries interact; the planner gets the ego query from MotionFormer, three learned command embeddings and the BEV feature, cross-attends the BEV in 3 decoder layers and regresses 6 steps (3 s). Inference-only occupancy optimisation picks the candidate minimising coordinate deviation + lambda_obs x Gaussian occupancy penalty (d = 5, sigma = 1, lambda_coord 1, lambda_obs 5).
formulation: BEV segmentation map not passed to the planner; max-pool over command-embedded modalities builds the plan query.
input: multi-view BEV features, command.
output: 3 s plan; panoptic map; motion and occupancy.
training: stage 1 tracking + mapping about 6 epochs; stage 2 end-to-end 20 epochs; image backbone gradient stopped in stage 1, image backbone and BEV encoder frozen in stage 2 (as read on the page); no other detaching described.
differentiable: partial - gradients reach map queries only through MotionFormer attention; matching discrete.
results: Table 2 (avg L2 / collision): no intermediate tasks (row 10) 1.131 m / 0.773 %; full UniAD (row 12) 1.004 / 0.430; the planning table does not isolate the map module; Table 10: occupancy optimisation lowers collision but raises L2 (0.44 -> 0.54 at 1 s); minADE 0.751 -> 0.736 when mapping is added to tracking + motion.
compute: 125.0 M parameters, 1.8 FPS on an A100 (numbers from the SparseDrive comparison).
code: https://github.com/OpenDriveLab/UniAD (v2.0 branch: mmdet3d 1.x, torch 2.x per README)
fit_to_us: baseline - effort L - the planner design (BEV cross-attention + command) is plain, the mmcv stack is the obstacle.
compat_needs: map queries with positions; BEV feature.
compat_conflicts: Hungarian matching; frozen BEV encoder in stage 2.

name: MAP (plan-enhancing online mapping + ego-status-guided planning)
papers: MAP: End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Map-Assisted Planning (Yin et al., ICCVW 2025) https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.13926
idea: Planning query Q_map = cross-attention of the mapping module's memory features with the ego-status embedding; a parallel branch Q_plan = cross-attention of BEV features with ego status; a weight adapter alpha in [0,1] (sigmoid of a 64-d vector from ego status + command) fuses Q_fused = alpha Q_plan + (1 - alpha) Q_map. The mapping module receives gradients from the mapping loss and from the trajectory loss through Q_map.
formulation: built on UniV2X (BEVFormer BEV, Panoptic SegFormer mapping), tracking / motion / occupancy removed; 5 s horizon (10 steps); loss = collision (BEV box overlap) + ADE + adaptive L2 / collision / off-road terms (weights not given); only the fused trajectory is supervised.
input: BEV features, mapping memory, ego status (CAN bus), command.
training: initialised from UniV2X stage-1 checkpoint; regime: imitation.
differentiable: yes (explicit statement of gradient into the mapping module).
results: val L2 / collision / off-road: UniV2X (retrained) 3.46 / 0.34 / 0.74, MAP 2.48 / 0.94 / 0.89 (collision and off-road higher than the baseline on validation); test leaderboard MAP L2 2.56, collision 0.96, off-road 0.39 vs UniV2X 3.07 / 0.71 / 0.89. Ablation (data subsampled to 1/5): w/o plan-enhancing mapping 3.22 / 1.35 / 1.13; w/o ego-guided branch 3.52 / 0.45 / 1.35; full 2.88 / 2.48 / 0.45.
compute: 2 x A800, about 50 h; transmission cost 1.69e5 BPS vs 8.09e5.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort S - mapping memory as planner query and an ego-status-dependent fusion weight are simple, but collision got worse.
compat_needs: dense mapping memory features.
compat_conflicts: cooperative-driving pipeline; different dataset.
tried_before: E119 / E121 (planner loss into route head / positions: no gain).

name: UMPE (map prior encoder with confidence-biased attention, used with VAD)
papers: Unified Map Prior Encoder for Mapping and Planning (arXiv 2605.02762; authors not read) https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02762
idea: One prior encoder for HD vectors, OSM vectors, satellite tiles and rasterised SD maps. Vector priors get SE(2) pre-alignment, multi-frequency sinusoidal point encoding and a 6-layer transformer producing tokens + confidences; BEV queries attend with dual cross-attention carrying a log-confidence bias, then presence-normalised channel gating. Raster priors: ResNet-18 with FiLM and grid_sample micro-alignment.
formulation: merge X = LN(Y) + alpha W LN(Z), W zero-initialised, alpha ramps 0 to about 0.6; source dropout p = 0.3.
input: priors + BEV query features.
output: augmented BEV feature for MapTRv2 / MapQR mapping and for VAD's planning decoder.
training: from scratch with a two-stage curriculum and separate learning rates for prior branches; whether planning gradients reach the prior encoder is not confirmed.
differentiable: yes (the confidence bias is additive in the attention logits).
results: planning with VAD: avg L2 0.72 -> 0.42 m, collision 0.22 -> 0.12 % (open loop only; no boundary metric, no NAVSIM); no planner-input noise test.
compute: planning runs 60 epochs on 8 x A800.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort S - the log-confidence additive attention bias is the soft form of our validity mask.
compat_needs: per-token confidence.
compat_conflicts: only VAD tested for planning; SparseDrive / UniAD / DiffusionDrive appear only as table baselines.
tried_before: E40 / E48 (map prior at the grid, learned registration) are the closest.

name: Topology-conditioning token for end-to-end planners (GT vs predicted topology)
papers: Plug-and-Play Traffic Element Awareness for End-to-End Autonomous Driving (arXiv 2608.18035; authors not read) https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18035
idea: Traffic elements (4 light states, 9 sign classes lifted to 3-D) and the ego-centric topology (centre-line-to-centre-line and centre-line-to-element relations of OpenLane-V2) are rendered as a sentence, encoded by a frozen BERT-base (about 110 M parameters) into queries and concatenated with the planner's BEV queries.
formulation: ego lane found from the ego position; LCLC gives ego-related centre-lines, LCTE the elements governing the ego lane; Q_plan = [Q_bev; Q_topo]; traffic-element 3-D centres from 2-D detection + UniDepthv2 + lidar.
input: lane subgraph (as text) + BEV queries of the base planner.
output: planner trajectory (base planners VAD, Orion on nuScenes; LTF, DiffusionDrive, DrivoR on NAVSIM; VAD, DriveTransformer-Large on Bench2Drive).
training: planners fine-tuned with the extra tokens (details not read).
differentiable: no through the text rendering and the frozen BERT; gradient reaches the planner only.
sensors_data: nuScenes (OpenLane-V2 annotations), NAVSIM (traffic elements only), Bench2Drive (GT topology).
results: nuScenes with VAD (ego scope, BERT encoder): GT topology avg L2 0.62 m / collision 0.16 %; topology predicted by TopoMLP 0.62 / 0.16 (identical); baseline VAD 0.72 / 0.22; full method 0.60 / 0.17; Orion 0.34 / 0.37 -> 0.26 / 0.23. Bench2Drive driving score VAD 42.3 -> 56.4, DriveTransformer-Large 63.46 -> 68.29 (traffic elements and topology combined).
compute: BERT 110 M parameters (frozen); rest not read.
fit_to_us: reuse_idea - effort S - a graph summary as one conditioning token is cheap; on nuScenes open loop the planner cannot tell GT from predicted topology, so the metric does not resolve graph quality.
compat_needs: a text or vector summary of the ego-relevant subgraph.
compat_conflicts: needs a text encoder; topology comes from OpenLane-V2 annotations, not from nuScenes map-expansion lanes.

name: Producing and Leveraging Online Map Uncertainty in Trajectory Prediction
papers: Producing and Leveraging Online Map Uncertainty in Trajectory Prediction (Gu et al., CVPR 2024) https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16439
idea: Online mapping heads (MapTR, MapTRv2 incl. a centre-line variant, StreamMapNet) output a Laplace location and scale per vertex; predictors (HiVT, DenseTNT) take (mu, b, class probabilities) as vertex features. It provides a ready nuScenes pipeline that scores a predicted centre-line map by downstream prediction.
formulation: vertex (x, y) = two independent Laplace; loss sum of log(2b) + |v - mu| / b (regression weight 0.03 for MapTR / MapTRv2, 2 for StreamMapNet); std = sqrt 2 b; coordinates ego-relative, scene rotated to heading "up"; DenseTNT (VectorNet lane encoder) concatenates uncertainty to the vertex vector; HiVT changes from a vector set to a point set and doubles the node dimension; no resampling or ordering described.
input: online vector map (vertices with scale and class probabilities), agent histories.
output: agent trajectories (3 s from 2 s of history).
training: staged; no end-to-end mapping + prediction (the "up to 50 %" claim concerns faster convergence of the predictor, e.g. DenseTNT 88 -> 44 epochs; the table label -22 % for the centre-line row does not match 99 -> 7 epochs).
differentiable: yes inside each stage; no gradient from prediction to mapping.
sensors_data: nuScenes (500 / 200 / 150 scenes), 2 Hz upsampled to 10 Hz; mAP at Chamfer 0.5 / 1.0 / 1.5 m.
